q: Lycan names two reasons the Cartesian first-person perspective suddenly lost dominance mid-20th century. One was:
a: Logical positivism's verification theory of meaning
w: The discovery of the pineal gland's real function
Descartes' own late retraction of his dualism
The invention of the first digital computers
e: The impact of logical positivism and the verification theory of meaning. Intersubjective verifiability became the criterion of meaning. The other reason was a set of pressing objections to dualism.

q: Which is NOT one of Lycan's four objections to Cartesian dualism?
a: Minds are divisible, so they can't be simple substances
w: Immaterial minds fit poorly with the scientific picture and aren't needed to explain behavior
It's anomalous for evolution to suddenly create immaterial minds
Immaterial mind-body causation would violate conservation laws
e: The four objections are: fits ill with science, evolution/development, the interaction problem, and conservation laws.

q: What did Descartes suggest as a model for how something immaterial could act on a body?
a: Gravity
w: Magnetism
Light
Heat
e: Lycan notes it's a poor model: gravity is intangible but still spatial in nature.

q: Analytical behaviorism claims that 'Leo is in pain' means:
a: He behaves, or is disposed to behave, in pain-ish ways
w: Leo's C-fibers are firing in a particular pattern
Leo's immaterial soul is experiencing a sensation
Leo is in a functional state that causes wincing
e: Leo is behaving, or is disposed to behave, in a wincing and groaning way. Associated with Carnap and Ryle. Mental ascriptions mean things about behavioral responses or dispositions.

q: Any behaviorist will subscribe to the Turing Test because they hold that:
a: Psychological differences can't outrun behavior
w: Machines can never genuinely think or feel
Only verbal behavior matters for having a mind
Brains are irrelevant to how we behave
e: Organisms whose actual and hypothetical behavior is identical are psychologically alike.

q: The inverted spectrum (from Locke) is an objection to behaviorism because:
a: Identical behavior could hide different color experiences
w: People can't actually perceive colors at all
Color experiences are simply states of the brain
It shows that behavior causes experience, not vice versa
e: Two people could behave identically yet differ in their color experiences. When you see red you might have the experience I have when I see green, with no behavioral difference.

q: 'Leo would shun parsnips only if he doesn't want to die.' This shows behaviorist analyses are:
a: Circular, because they presuppose other mental states
w: Perfectly adequate as translations of mental talk
Dualist theories presented in disguise
Only about verbal behavior, not other actions
e: Circular or radically incomplete, since they presuppose other mental states. Translating a belief into behavior requires assumptions about desires and other beliefs (Chisholm, Geach).

q: Who proposed the identity theory as a middle way between dualism and behaviorism?
a: U.T. Place and J.J.C. Smart
w: Putnam and Fodor
Ryle and Carnap
Churchland and Feyerabend
e: Mental states are genuinely inner and episodic (against behaviorism) but neurophysiological (against dualism).

q: Lewis and Armstrong's deductive argument for the identity theory says: pain is by definition whatever occupies a certain causal role, and science will find that a neural state occupies it. Therefore:
a: Pain is that neural state
w: Pain is a behavioral disposition
Pain is non-physical
Pain has no causal role
e: Mental terms are defined causally (the terms of 'folk psychology'), and the role-occupant is found empirically.

q: 'Water = H2O' and 'lightning = electrical discharge' are examples of identities that are:
a: Synthetic and a posteriori
w: Analytic and a priori
True by definition
Mere correlations
e: Synthetic and a posteriori: discovered empirically, not by meaning. So the identity theorist doesn't claim 'pain' MEANS brain state. It's a scientific identity, like the Morning Star being Venus.

q: Putnam and Fodor's objection to type identity theory is that it commits:
a: Species chauvinism
w: Liberalism
Substance dualism
Logical behaviorism
e: Species chauvinism: only creatures with C-fibers could feel pain. Why must any pain-feeling organism be made of the same chemicals as us?

q: According to machine functionalism, the pain TYPE is identified with:
a: An abstract functional role
w: The firing of C-fibers
Wincing and groaning behavior
An immaterial sensation
e: Pain TOKENS are identical to particular neural states (token physicalism). The type is the role those states play.

q: Unlike behaviorism and the identity theory, functionalism:
a: Doesn't strictly entail that minds are physical
w: Requires that minds be immaterial substances
Identifies minds directly with outward behavior
Denies that minds can be multiply realized
e: Non-physical minds could in principle realize the right program.

q: In homuncular functionalism, a 'homunculus' is:
a: A part defined by its function, broken into sub-parts
w: A tiny person who literally lives inside the brain
An immaterial soul that controls the body
A single row in a Turing machine's table
e: A component identified by its function, itself broken down into sub-components until neurophysiology is reached. Like explaining a car by its carburetor, fuel line, etc. Systems are hierarchically organized (Fodor, Dennett, Cummins).

q: Why is machine functionalism's criterion of 'realization' (one-to-one correspondence) too liberal?
a: Almost anything has motions that map onto a program
w: Nothing could ever realize a program exactly
Only digital computers can realize programs
It requires a biological brain to realize anything
e: Almost any physical object has some molecular motions that map onto a given program. The proposed fix is a teleological requirement: the state must play its role FOR the organism, as its biological purpose.

q: On the etiological account of biological function, a heart's function is to pump blood because:
a: Hearts were selected for pumping blood
w: A designer intended hearts to pump blood
Pumping blood is the only thing hearts can do
People generally believe that hearts pump blood
e: Hearts were selected for pumping blood in the past. A trait has function F because it was selected for doing F (Wright, Millikan).

q: Brentano distinguished psychological phenomena from physical objects on the grounds that psychological phenomena:
a: Are directed at objects, even non-existent ones
w: Have mass and take up space
Can be divided into smaller parts
Are always fully conscious to the subject
e: Are directed upon objects, even non-existent ones (intentionality). How could a physical state be 'about' King Arthur or Sherlock Holmes? Bricks aren't about anything.

q: Nagel and Jackson's anti-materialist argument appeals to:
a: Knowing what a sensation is like requires having it
w: The law of conservation of energy in the brain
Multiple realizability of mental states
The results of the Turing Test for machines
e: A disparity in knowledge: you only know what a sensation is like by having it. No amount of third-person scientific information gives you 'what it is like'. Functionalists reply it's an ability, or a fallacy with Leibniz's Law.

q: Kripke argued against identity theory using:
a: Modal distinctions about necessary identity
w: Evolutionary biology and natural selection
Behavioral experiments on animals and people
The theory of Turing machines and computation
e: Modal distinctions: mental items aren't NECESSARILY identical to neural ones, so they aren't identical at all. True identities are necessary. Since pain without C-fibers seems possible, pain ≠ C-fiber firing.

q: Putnam's Twin Earth examples show that propositional attitude contents are:
a: 'Wide': not fixed by what's in the head
w: 'Narrow': fully fixed by brain state
Identical to a person's behavior
Non-existent, strictly speaking
e: 'Wide': not determined by the total state of the subject's head. Molecule-for-molecule twins could differ in beliefs. That's a problem if functional roles are narrow.

q: Dennett is an instrumentalist about beliefs and desires, meaning:
a: Ascriptions predict well but don't describe inner causes
w: Beliefs and desires don't exist and all ascriptions are false
Beliefs and desires are identical to particular brain states
Beliefs and desires are states of an immaterial mind
e: Belief/desire ascriptions are often true and predictive, but don't describe inner causal mechanisms. Like the 'average American homeowner' with 2.2 children. Ascribing a belief is like moving beads on an abacus.

q: Davidson's anomalous monism differs from Dennett's instrumentalism in that it:
a: It holds mental tokens are physical causes
w: It denies that any mental states exist
It's a form of substance dualism
It identifies mental types with neural types
e: Endorses token physicalism and holds mental tokens are causes. It rejects type-reduction of the attitudes on epistemological grounds, but mental tokens are physical causes.

q: Eliminativists, identity theorists and functionalists all agree that:
a: Mental items, if anything, are real inner causes
w: Folk psychology is true and needs no revision
Mental ascriptions are mere calculational devices
Dualism is correct about the nature of mind
e: Mental items, if anything, are real inner-causal states; they disagree on whether folk categories match them. They all scorn the instrumentalist's 'sleazy evasion'. Lycan calls the three views an 'eternal triangle'.

q: Who was the first to openly argue that folk psychology's categories fail to capture anything real?
a: Paul Feyerabend
w: Paul Churchland
Richard Rorty
Gilbert Ryle
e: Feyerabend (1963) attracted little following. Churchland (1981) later resurrected eliminativism.

q: Paul Churchland's main argument for eliminativism is from:
a: Folk psychology's poverty, like alchemy's
w: Searle's Chinese Room thought experiment
Locke's inverted spectrum example
Conservation laws in physics
e: The poverty of folk psychology, compared to abandoned theories like alchemy. Bad theories get abandoned, and folk psychology has done as badly as alchemy did.

q: One way to resist eliminativism (Ryle, Wittgenstein) is to deny that:
a: Folk psychology is a theory at all
w: The brain is the organ of the mind
Science can tell us about minds
Behavior can be publicly observed
e: Others (Kitcher; Horgan & Woodward) argue instead that it's not a failed or bad theory.
